title: Worst-case logarithmic dynamic planar convex hulls
formal: Does there exist a deterministic data structure maintaining a finite set \(P\subset\mathbb R^2\) under point insertion and deletion, using \(O(1+|P|)\) space, with \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time for every update and every extreme-point query? Here \(n\) is the larger set size immediately before and after the operation. An extreme-point query supplies \(u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\) and returns a point maximizing \(\langle u,p\rangle\) over \(p\in P\), or an empty marker.
definitions: The set is initially empty. Insertions supply distinct points; deletions name a present point by a stable handle returned at insertion. Ties may be resolved by any fixed deterministic rule. Use an algebraic real RAM: exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value and comparisons each cost one step, as do constant-size record and pointer operations; no floor, bit extraction from reals or arbitrary-precision encoding operation is supplied. A point, pointer or scalar occupies one cell. One finite program must handle every finite valid online sequence, without advance knowledge, with universal constants in the bounds. Only a maximizing point is returned, not an explicit list of all hull vertices.
why: This asks whether optimal dynamic geometric query performance can be guaranteed for individual updates rather than only averaged over a sequence.

context_blocks.text: Brodal and Jacob achieve logarithmic amortized insertion and deletion with logarithmic worst-case extreme-point queries in linear space. Their concluding questions explicitly include worst-case logarithmic updates.
A single update may change many hull vertices. The maintained query representation avoids requiring the entire polygon to be output after each change.

sentences: A planar point set changes by insertion and deletion.
A query asks for a point farthest in a supplied direction.
The target is linear storage and logarithmic time for each individual operation.
The known optimal update guarantee is amortized over a sequence.
The question isolates whether geometric maintenance must sometimes cause expensive update spikes.
